title: Vectors and matrices
summary: Vectors as arrows and lists of numbers, the dot product, norms and cosine similarity, matrix shapes and multiplication, and the special matrices (identity, inverse, determinant) that NOAI asks about.
syllabus: Vectors, dot product, norms (L1, L2), cosine similarity
Identity, inverse, determinant, trace, symmetric matrices

lessons.title: Vectors: arrows and lists of numbers
lessons.summary: A vector is both an arrow in space and a list of numbers; adding and scaling work the same way in both pictures.
objectives: You can read a vector as an arrow and as a list
You can add vectors and multiply them by a number
You can describe a data point (e.g. a student's marks) as a vector

concepts.name: A vector is an arrow and a list
concepts.explain: Start with a point on graph paper: going 3 right and 4 up is the arrow (3, 4). The same list of numbers can store anything with several measurements, such as a house's size, age and price. A vector with n numbers lives in n-dimensional space.
concepts.analogy: Directions from Bishan MRT to your school, '3 blocks east, 4 blocks north', are a vector: one instruction made of two numbers.

visual.shows: A Plot grid with an arrow from the origin to a draggable tip, with its components drawn as dashed horizontal and vertical legs and the list [x, y] shown beside it.
visual.interaction: Drag the tip; the list updates live. Toggle 'data mode' to relabel the axes as 'hours studied' and 'score' so the arrow becomes a student record.
visual.aha: The arrow picture and the list of numbers are the same object, so geometry and data are interchangeable.

concepts.name: Adding and scaling vectors
concepts.explain: To add vectors, add matching components; geometrically you place the arrows tip to tail. Multiplying by a number (a scalar) stretches or shrinks the arrow, and a negative number flips it.
concepts.analogy: Taking the MRT 3 stops east and then a bus 2 stops north lands you where the combined trip would; walking the same route twice is scaling by 2.

visual.shows: Two draggable arrows u and v, the tip-to-tail construction, and the sum u + v as a third arrow; a scalar slider produces c·u as a ghost arrow.
visual.interaction: Drag u and v; slide c from -2 to 3 and watch c·u stretch, shrink, vanish at 0 and flip when negative.
visual.aha: Vector arithmetic is just component-wise arithmetic, which is why NumPy can add whole arrays at once.

lessons.title: Dot product, norms and cosine similarity
lessons.summary: How to measure length, distance and 'how much two vectors point the same way'.
objectives: You can compute a dot product by hand
You can compute L1 and L2 norms and the distance between vectors
You can compute and interpret cosine similarity

concepts.name: The dot product measures alignment
concepts.explain: Multiply matching components and add: [1, 2]·[3, 4] = 1×3 + 2×4 = 11. Geometrically, a·b = |a||b|cos θ, so it is large and positive when the vectors point the same way, zero when they are perpendicular (orthogonal) and negative when they point apart.
concepts.analogy: Pushing a trolley at an angle: only the part of your push along the trolley's direction moves it; the dot product measures that useful part.

visual.shows: Two draggable arrows, the shadow (projection) of one onto the other drawn as a thick segment, the angle arc, and a readout of a·b computed both ways (component sum and |a||b|cos θ).
visual.interaction: Drag either arrow; the shadow and value change colour from positive (green) through zero (perpendicular) to negative (red).
visual.aha: The sign of the dot product tells you at a glance whether two vectors agree, disagree or are unrelated.

concepts.name: Norms: different ways to measure length
concepts.explain: The L2 norm is ordinary length by Pythagoras, so ||[3, 4]||₂ = √(9 + 16) = 5. The L1 norm adds absolute values, |3| + |4| = 7, like walking along a street grid. The distance between two points is the norm of their difference.
concepts.analogy: L2 is the crow's flight over HDB blocks; L1 is the taxi route that must follow the roads.

visual.shows: The 'unit balls' of L1 (diamond), L2 (circle) and L∞ (square) drawn together, with a draggable point and its three norms listed.
visual.interaction: Drag the point; watch it cross each shape's boundary when that norm equals 1. Toggle to show the L1 path along the grid versus the straight L2 path.
visual.aha: Different norms are different rulers; the diamond's sharp corners will later explain why L1 regularisation makes weights exactly zero.

concepts.name: Cosine similarity
concepts.explain: Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both lengths: cos θ = a·b / (|a||b|). It ignores how long the vectors are and keeps only direction, giving 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular and -1 for opposite.
concepts.analogy: Two playlists with the same mix of genres are similar even if one is ten times longer; cosine similarity compares the mix, not the size.

visual.shows: A dial from -1 to 1 driven by the angle between two arrows, with a side panel of three tiny word-count vectors for short documents.
visual.interaction: Rotate one arrow; stretch it with a length slider and see cosine stay fixed while the dot product changes. Pick two documents to compare their cosine.
visual.aha: Cosine similarity is about direction only, which is why search engines and RAG use it to compare documents of different lengths.

checkpoint_focus: L2 norm via Pythagoras, L1 as sum of absolute values

lessons.title: Matrices, shapes and matrix multiplication
lessons.summary: Matrices as tables of numbers, the shape rule for multiplication and how each entry is a row-times-column dot product.
objectives: You can state the shape of a matrix and its transpose
You can decide whether two matrices can be multiplied and the result's shape
You can compute a small matrix product by hand
You can tell element-wise multiplication from matrix multiplication

concepts.name: Shapes and the inner-dimension rule
concepts.explain: A matrix with m rows and n columns has shape m×n. You can multiply A (m×n) by B (n×p) only when the inner numbers match, and the result has the outer shape m×p. The inner dimension disappears because it is summed over.
concepts.analogy: Like train couplings: two carriages join only if the coupling sizes match, and the joined train keeps the two outer ends.

visual.shows: Two domino tiles labelled with shapes (e.g. 3×2 and 2×4); when the inner numbers match they snap together and the result tile (3×4) appears, otherwise they bounce apart with the mismatch highlighted.
visual.interaction: Use steppers to change the four dimensions; try chains of three matrices.
visual.aha: You can check any matrix product (and most PyTorch shape errors) by looking only at the shapes.

concepts.name: Each entry is a row times a column
concepts.explain: Entry (i, j) of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. For a 2×2 product that is four dot products. Matrix-vector multiplication Ax is a weighted sum of A's columns, which is exactly what a neural-network layer computes.
concepts.analogy: A hawker's bill: each customer's row of orders times the column of prices gives that customer's total.

visual.shows: MatrixGrid views of A, B and AB with small integers; at each step the active row of A and column of B light up and the products and sum appear before filling the output cell.
visual.interaction: Step forward or back through every output cell, or click any output cell to jump to its computation; swap to B·A to compare.
visual.aha: Matrix multiplication is just many dot products arranged in a grid, and swapping the order usually changes the answer.

concepts.name: Transpose, and element-wise versus matrix product
concepts.explain: The transpose Aᵀ flips rows and columns, so a 2×3 matrix becomes 3×2 and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. Element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication multiplies matching entries and needs equal shapes; it is a different operation from the matrix product.
concepts.analogy: Transposing is turning a class timetable from 'days across, periods down' to 'periods across, days down': same data, swapped layout.

visual.shows: A 2×3 grid whose cells rotate about the main diagonal into a 3×2 grid; a second tab contrasts A∘B (cell by cell) with A@B (row by column) on the same two matrices.
visual.interaction: Play the flip animation; switch tabs and hover cells to see which inputs produced each output.
visual.aha: '*' and '@' look similar in code but mean completely different things; mixing them up is a classic exam trap.

lessons.title: Identity, inverse, determinant and trace
lessons.summary: The special matrices and single numbers that describe what a matrix does, including when it cannot be undone.
objectives: You can recognise identity, diagonal and symmetric matrices
You can compute a 2×2 determinant and inverse
You can explain what a zero determinant (singular matrix) means

concepts.name: The determinant is an area scale factor
concepts.explain: A 2×2 matrix maps the unit square to a parallelogram; its determinant ad − bc is the signed area of that parallelogram. A determinant of 0 means the square is squashed flat onto a line, so information is lost.
concepts.analogy: Like a photocopier zoom: a determinant of 2 doubles every area, 0.5 halves it, and 0 squashes the page into a line.

visual.shows: A grid with the unit square and its image parallelogram, the two column vectors as draggable arrows, and det = ad − bc with the area shaded (colour flips when the orientation flips).
visual.interaction: Drag the column vectors; make them parallel to watch the area collapse to zero and the 'singular' badge appear.
visual.aha: det = 0 means some direction is crushed, which is exactly why a singular matrix has no inverse.

concepts.name: Identity and inverse undo each other
concepts.explain: The identity matrix I has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere and leaves every vector unchanged, so AI = IA = A. The inverse A⁻¹ undoes A, so A⁻¹A = I. For a 2×2 matrix, A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))·[[d, −b], [−c, a]], which only exists when ad − bc ≠ 0. There is no matrix division: 'A ÷ B' is not defined, and you multiply by B⁻¹ instead when it exists.
concepts.analogy: Encrypting a message and decrypting it: the decryption key is the inverse, and doing both gets you back to the original (the identity).

visual.shows: A small shape (an arrow-shaped 'house') transformed by A, then by A⁻¹, returning to the start; the matrices are shown in MatrixGrid.
visual.interaction: Step through apply A, apply A⁻¹; edit A to make it singular and see the 'no inverse' step fail.
visual.aha: Undoing is only possible when nothing was squashed, linking inverse to determinant.

concepts.name: Symmetric, diagonal and trace
concepts.explain: A symmetric matrix equals its own transpose (entry i,j equals entry j,i); covariance matrices are always symmetric. A diagonal matrix only has entries on the main diagonal and simply scales each axis. The trace is the sum of the diagonal entries.
concepts.analogy: A symmetric matrix is like a table of distances between MRT stations: the distance from A to B equals the distance from B to A.

visual.shows: A 3×3 MatrixGrid with editable cells and badges (identity, diagonal, symmetric, singular) that light up when the matrix qualifies, plus readouts for trace and determinant.
visual.interaction: Edit cells or click presets; mirror-highlight shows entry (i,j) and (j,i) together.
visual.aha: These properties are visible patterns in the grid, so many MCQs can be answered by inspection rather than calculation.

checkpoint_focus: Singular means det = 0 and no inverse
